procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and decree dated November 29, 1960 of the Madras High Court in Appeal Suit No. 207 of 1957.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court upheld the contention of Natarajan Chettiar (respondent No. 3) that properties in schedule D were not liable to be partitioned. The High Court heard the appeal (Appeal Suit No. 207 of 1957) and issued a judgment and decree on November 29, 1960.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants appealed the judgment and decree of the Madras High Court to the Supreme Court after the High Court granted a certificate to do so.

directions: The appeal therefore fails and is hereby dismissed with costs to the plaintiff-respondent.

issue.issue_text: whether the plaintiff-respondent was the son of Rangaswami Chettiar

facts: The trial court and the High Court both found that the plaintiff-respondent was the son of Rangaswami Chettiar, creating a "concurrent finding of fact."
The appellants (the deceased's other wives) argued against this, pointing to a notice where Rangaswami Chettiar had denied paternity.
The plaintiff's mother, Lakshmiammal, testified that she had not left her husband and that the plaintiff was his son. The High Court did not disbelieve her testimony.
Evidence showed that even if Lakshmiammal was living separately, her father's house was only a furlong away from Rangaswami Chettiar's house.
law: The Supreme Court stated that it ordinarily does not interfere with a concurrent finding of fact from lower courts.
The Court relied on Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, which establishes a "conclusive presumption" that a child born during a valid marriage is the legitimate son of the husband.
To rebut this presumption, the party denying paternity has a "heavy burden" to prove that the husband and wife had "no access to each other at any time when he could have been begotten."
application: The Court reasoned that the notice from Rangaswami Chettiar denying paternity was not strong enough evidence to overcome the conclusive presumption of Section 112.
The appellants were required to prove that Rangaswami Chettiar had no access to Lakshmiammal during the period of conception.
The Court found that the evidence, particularly the fact that the couple lived only a furlong apart, fell "far short" of proving non-access.
The Court accepted the mother's testimony, which had not been disbelieved by the High Court, as further support.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants had completely failed to prove non-access and therefore could not rebut the strong legal presumption of legitimacy. Consequently, the Court upheld the findings of the lower courts and held that the plaintiff-respondent was the legitimate son of Rangaswami Chettiar.

issue.issue_text: whether the deed of gift was valid

facts: A husband, R, executed a deed of gift for some ancestral immovable property in favor of his second wife.

The wife (the donee-appellant) argued that the gift was valid because it was a reasonable portion of the property, made out of love and affection, and was intended to fulfill a pious obligation to carry out the wishes of her husband's father.
law: Under Hindu law, a father or managing member of a family can make a gift of a reasonable portion of ancestral immovable property for "pious purposes."
A gift of ancestral property to a daughter at the time of her marriage is considered a pious purpose.

There is no authority or precedent in Hindu law to support the proposition that a husband can gift ancestral immovable property to his wife, or that a father-in-law can gift it to his daughter-in-law.
A gift from a husband to a wife out of love and affection is not permitted under Hindu law if the property is ancestral and immovable.
application: The Court refused to extend the scope of "pious purposes" to include a gift from a husband to his wife.

The Court distinguished this case from a gift to a daughter, reasoning that a daughter-in-law becomes a member of the new family and acquires rights to the property, unlike a daughter who is leaving her father's family.

The Court rejected the argument that the husband was fulfilling a pious obligation from his father, stating that even the father-in-law himself would not have been competent to make such a gift of ancestral immovable property.
The Court found no legal basis to uphold a gift of ancestral immovable property from a husband to his wife made simply out of affection.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the deed of gift was not valid because a gift of ancestral immovable property from a husband to his wife is not permitted under Hindu law, as it does not qualify as a "pious purpose."

issue.issue_text: The scope of the expression 'pious pwposes' cannot be extended to include such gifts.

facts: A husband made a gift of ancestral immovable property to his wife.
The wife (the donee-appellant) argued that this gift should be considered valid because it was made for 'pious purposes', specifically out of love and affection.
law: Under Hindu Law, a Hindu father or managing member of a family has the power to make a gift of a reasonable portion of ancestral immovable property for 'pious purposes'.
The term 'pious purposes' is generally understood to mean gifts for charitable or religious purposes.

The Supreme Court had previously extended the meaning of 'pious purposes' to include a reasonable gift of ancestral immovable property from a father to his daughter, viewing it as a fulfillment of a moral obligation.
application: The Court was asked to further extend the definition of 'pious purposes' to include a gift of ancestral immovable property from a husband to his wife, made out of affection.

The Court noted that while it had previously extended the definition to include gifts to a daughter, it could find no precedent or case law upholding a gift of ancestral immovable property from a husband to his wife.

The Court explicitly stated, "We see no reason to extend the scope of the words 'pious purposes' beyond what has already been done in the two decisions of this Court to which reference has been made."

It distinguished the case of a daughter, who is leaving the family upon marriage, from that of a wife, who becomes a member of the husband's family and may acquire rights to the property in other ways.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a gift of ancestral immovable property made by a husband to his wife out of affection does not fall under the scope of 'pious purposes'. The Court refused to extend the definition to include such gifts, concluding that they are not permitted under Hindu Law, and therefore the gift was invalid.

law.law_text: Under Hindu Law, a father or any other managing member of a family has the power to make a gift of ancestral immovable property only within reasonable limits and for 'pious purposes'.

A gift of ancestral immovable property by a father to his own daughter at the time of her marriage is considered a 'pious purpose' because she is leaving the family and it is the father's duty to provide for her.

While gifts made in token of love by a father-in-law to a daughter-in-law are permitted and become her 'stridhan' (personal property), this rule does not extend to gifts of ancestral immovable property.

application.application_text: The Court found no authority or precedent in Hindu law to support the proposition that a father-in-law can gift ancestral immovable property to his daughter-in-law.

The Court reasoned that unlike a daughter who is leaving the family, a daughter-in-law becomes a member of the father-in-law's family after marriage and would be entitled to the ancestral property in her own right under certain circumstances. Therefore, her case stands on a "very different footing".

The Court concluded that a gift from a father-in-law to a daughter-in-law at her marriage cannot, by any stretch of reasoning, be considered a 'pious purpose' that would justify gifting ancestral immovable property.
To reconcile the rules, the Court stated that if a father-in-law gifts immovable property to his daughter-in-law as stridhan, it can only be his self-acquired property, not ancestral property.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition, holding that a father-in-law is not competent under Hindu law to make a gift of ancestral immovable property to his daughter-in-law at the time of her marriage because such a gift does not qualify as a 'pious purpose'.

respondent_arguments: The plaintiff was the son of Rangaswami Chettiar and was entitled to a half share in the joint family properties.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Hindu law, a gift of ancestral immovable property by a husband to his wife out of love and affection is not valid. A father-in-law is not competent to make a gift of ancestral immovable property to his daughter-in-law, as it is not a pious purpose, and consequently, a son has no pious obligation to make such a gift to fulfill his father's wishes.
obiter: The Hindu law texts conferred a right upon a daughter or a sister to have a share in the family property at the time of partition, which crystallized into a moral obligation for the father or his representative to make a valid gift by way of reasonable provision.
The rule that a father-in-law can make a gift to a daughter-in-law applies only to property that is not ancestral immovable property.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A gift of ancestral immovable property by a husband to his wife, even if made out of affection or in purported fulfillment of his father's wishes, is not permitted under Hindu Law. The scope of 'pious purposes,' which allows for gifts of ancestral property, cannot be extended to include such transfers, as the position of a daughter-in-law who joins the family is fundamentally different from that of a daughter who is leaving it upon marriage.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a gift of ancestral immovable property falls within the scope of 'pious purposes' as defined by Hindu law and interpreted by prior court decisions. The court explicitly states its refusal to expand this scope: 'We see no reason to extend the scope of the words "pious purposes" beyond what has already been done in the two decisions of this Court to which reference has been made.'
why_appellant_lost: The argument that a gift of ancestral immovable property from a husband to a wife out of affection is valid was rejected because the court found no precedent for it: 'we have not been referred to a single case where a gift by a husband to his wife of immovable ancestral property if made, has been upheld... no such gift is permitted under Hindu Law insofar as inunovable ancestral property is concerned.'

The contention that the gift was a 'pious obligation' to fulfill the father-in-law's wishes failed because the father-in-law himself lacked the authority to make such a gift. The court reasoned that one cannot be obligated to do what is legally impermissible: 'we cannot see how what the father-in-law himself could not do could be made into a pious obligation on the son as is claimed in this case, for that would be permitting indirectly what is not permitted under Hindu law directly.'

The court explicitly rejected the idea that a gift to a daughter-in-law at the time of marriage constitutes a 'pious purpose': 'we cannot see how a gift by the father-in-law to the daughter-in-law at the time of marriage can by any stretch of reasoning be called a pious purpose, whatever may be the position of a gift by the father or his representative to a daughter at the time of her marriage.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the gift was invalid was upheld because the court affirmed the established principle that Hindu law does not permit a husband to gift ancestral immovable property to his wife.

The court agreed that the gift did not fall under the exception for 'pious purposes,' refusing to extend the doctrine to cover gifts made out of affection between spouses or to fulfill a father-in-law's wishes.

The court's reasoning supported the respondent's case by establishing that since a father-in-law cannot validly gift ancestral immovable property to a daughter-in-law, no pious obligation can arise for his son to do so on his behalf.
policy_considerations: The court distinguished the social and legal positions of a daughter and a daughter-in-law to justify the different treatment of gifts. A gift to a daughter upon marriage is permissible as she is leaving her father's family: 'One can understand such a gift being made to a daughter when she is leaving the family of her father.'

Conversely, a gift to a daughter-in-law is not considered a pious purpose because she becomes a member of the new family and acquires rights to its property through that status: 'As a matter of fact the daughter-in-law becomes a memlicr of the family of her father-in-law after marriage and she would be entitled after marriage in her own right to the ancestml immovable property in certain circumstances, and clearly therefore her case stands on a very different footing from the case of a daughter.'
